This movie, along with Contempt, really shows Godard at his best. So the French New Wave movement initially was heavily influenced by stuff like Italian Neorealism. If you watch stuff like The 400 Blows or Breathless you’ll see filming on actual locations with simple stories, instead of filming in sets, often with handheld cameras.

However right from the start French directors go beyond strict realism, The 400 Blows for instance ends with a freeze frame, and Breathless features frequent jump cuts that call attention to themselves. 

By the time we get to Pierrot le Fou, Godard has enough experience that things start to get really interesting. Influenced by pop art, he has a vivid use of bright colors, his camera work moves beyond hand held shots to tracking shots, his editing is off the wall, the soundtrack adds and removes elements sometimes at random, it’s a lot. 

In terms of the story he’s influenced by classic Hollywood couple on the run stories but takes the narrative in absurd directions. It’s interesting though, Godard initially revered Hollywood, but at this time the escalation of the Vietnam War soured Godard’s feelings on America, which obviously comes through at points.
Wonderful insight. Thank you so much. Now I know the next two movies to put on my list.

Had to go back for an immediate rewatch, something I've only done twice previously. Was waaay less off the wall surreal than I got on the first watch. 

An absolute masterclass of film making. So excited to check out more. It's amazing how from one film, you can see his influence on so many people.

Please tell me the best route to explore more from here!

A Woman is a Woman almost feels like the precursor to Pierrot for me. Contempt is great, like the other commenter said! Those and Pierrot make up my top three for him.

Outside of Godard, Chabrol is another good new wave director (Les cousins is great). Truffaut (shoot the piano player, the whole Antoine Doinel saga), Varda (la pointe courte, Cleo 5 to 7), Malle (elevator to the gallows) — all very much worth watching.
Thank you so much! I can't wait to learn more about all your suggestions!

I think an enormous amount of the effect of ***Pierrot le Fou*** comes from the atomic-powered charisma of the two leads. I get the sense that Godard felt that he just needed to put them in front of a camera and the magic would happen regardless of what they did. 

Belmondo is at his vagabond best here, and if you like him here you should also see ***A bout de souffle*** (Breathless).

Meanwhile Anna Karina is just incredible, and for more of her you should check out ***Vivre sa vie*** (Living her life\[?\]) and ***Bande a part*** (Band of Outsiders). 

Without these two the effect of Godard's radical filmmaking might be less impactful. I'm thinking of ***Le Mépris*** (Contempt) where Brigitte Bardot is sensual but not as charismatic as Karina. 

Other than those, Godard's most radical work is a challenge. ***La Chinoise*** and ***One Plus One/Sympathy for the Devil*** are where he puts his Maoist radical politics into full effect.

In 1964, Jean-Luc Godard envisioned "Pierrot le fou" as a tale of obsessive desire, planning to adapt Lionel White's crime novel into a film depicting a man's infatuation with a young girl, ultimately leading to betrayal and tragedy. However, casting changes and personal turmoil reshaped the narrative. Godard's divorce from his wife, Anna Karina, altered the film's direction, turning it into a deeply personal outcry. The movie became a reflection of Godard's emotional turmoil, channeling resentment and pain over his failed marriage into the storyline, blurring the lines between art and reality.

When filming finally commenced in 1965, Godard faced a creative crisis. Struggling to find his cinematic bearings, he abandoned traditional storytelling methods, opting for fragmented images and disjointed sequences. This shift marked a departure from conventional cinema, reflecting Godard's attempt to evoke intense emotions through unconventional stylistic choices, mirroring his internal conflict amidst a rapidly changing world.

"Pierrot le fou" premiered to polarized reactions at the Venice Film Festival in 1965 but garnered critical acclaim from influential voices like Michel Cournot and Louis Aragon. Its fusion of self-destructive romanticism, artistic self-awareness, and boundary-defying narrative influenced a generation of filmmakers, heralding Godard's transition into more radical cinematic experiments while resonating as a cinematic reflection of an era rife with personal and societal upheaval
Please do! The French era around the 50s-60s is about as good as movies get in my opinion!

> ... and rule breaking ...

You say rule breaking. I say incomprehensible drivel. You have to know the rules before you can break them, and I'm not particularly convinced Godard could have made a conventional story with realistic believable characters to save his life.

Respect to your opinion. I hated the film right up until I fell in love with it. Also already mentioned that I'm not really educated in that school of filmmaking. Would be interested in your thoughts.

Ahhh, Pierrot le Fou, a mad swing of the cinematic pendulum! The French New Wave was nothing short of an earthquake in film history, a breath of fresh air, an enfant terrible. Godard was one of its chief architects, his work is a thrilling blend of aloof cool and warm passion, a moody mix that gets under your skin.

First of all, Pierrot le Fou has a very fragmented, disjointed narrative style. The edit skips, fast-forwards, cuts abruptly. Remember the jump cuts in Breathless? This is the same but cranked to 11. Part of Godard's rebellious vive contre le system! Breaking narrative rules, leading us down different paths, a non-linear storytelling approach. It was as innovative as it was bewildering.

The film is chock-full of references, in-jokes, and nods to literature, philosophy, and American pulp cinema. It's like an artistic fun-house mirror, it reflects Godard's own obsessions and fascinations, leading some to see it as his most autobiographical work.

Your reading of the first part and the tonal shift is spot on, the whiplash from giddy anarchy to tragic romance is certainly part of the film's challenging charm. The shift punctuates the free-wheeling adventure with an undercurrent of fatalism, which levels it out, balances it with melancholy - 'the party can't last forever' kinda feeling.  

Suffice it to say, you've embarked in one of the wildest rides in art-house cinema, enjoy!

Thank you so much for your response. And I believe you described my experience with this film perfectly with a fun house mirror. Also your writing style is amazing! 

Regarding your comment, I'm curious what in-jokes you're referring to. I feel like I picked up on a lot of the pop culture references, but likely missed some. After reading your comment, it does tell so much about Godaard. He really exposes himself in this. And we're better off for it.

Rule breaking, reflection on reality/reality of reflection, postmodern agitprop blah blah blah...no academic term or discourse can do it any justice. Beyond everything else, it's just so imaginative, so rich in colours and passion, so vulnerable in it's confessions and just so alive, it is everything I love about Godard and what his filmmaking stood for. In a utopian world, Godard's approach towards image and sound would be the norm, but it is what it is. 

Modern cinema is boring; bring back the new wave!!!
